C0.quote: A voting rule is a collective choice rule that maps preference profiles
C0.note: Compares single-winner voting rules (Condorcet-consistent, scoring, sequential scoring, approval) on polarized preference domains.

C1.quote: Property PPC holds if, for a given profile, a voting rule
C1.note: Main results establish which rules satisfy property PPC on each polarized profile (Table 4, Theorem 1). Numerical Saari-triangle examples in Appendix B are illustrations, not simulations.

C2.1.value: preference profiles; preference orderings / preference rankings; votes; approvals (AV)
C2.1.quote: A voting rule is a collective choice rule that maps preference profiles

C2.2.note: Strict rankings throughout; approval voting analysed in Sec. 4.4 ("It entails each voter being able to either approve (some) individual"), with approvals derived from rankings via cut-off levels.

C2.3.quote: voters’ top (best) preference is always identical with their votes
C2.3.note: Voters' preferences are referred to as distinct from their votes / what they submit.

C2.4.loc: Sec. 2 The model, p. 2; Sec. 4.3, p. 10
C2.4.quote: most of the other related papers, we neglect strategic considerations of voters
C2.4.note: The paper states that votes equal preferences (Sec. 2: top preference 'always identical with their votes'; Sec. 4.3: voters 'vote according to their original preference rankings') and justifies this by convention in prior work (Dasgupta and Maskin), which C3.3 codes as CONV, a reason; the remarks that voters may reconsider (Sec. 4.3) or that honest voting may not be compelling (Sec. 4.4) acknowledge a possibility that is then assumed away, not a model treating input and preference as separate objects.

C3.1.quote: our model neither accounts for decisions to abstain from voting nor strategic
C3.1.note: All analyses assume voters vote according to their preference rankings; the remark on moderates in Sec. 4.4 is commentary, not a strategic analysis.

C3.2.quote: we assume that all voters participate in all rounds and vote
C3.2.note: Sec. 2 also: 'we neglect strategic considerations of voters' and voters' top preference identical with their plurality votes.

C3.3.quote: As in Dasgupta and Maskin (2008) and most of the other
C3.3.note: The sincere-voting assumption is justified by reference to prior work; Sec. 4.3 adds only that the model does not account for strategic deliberation, and the plurality-vote identity is tied to neglecting menu dependency.

C4.1.quote: the consideration of preference intensities inferred from ordinal data.
C4.1.note: Applicability met: inputs are rankings (RANK) and the paper uses voters' 'preference intensities' (Borda/MIIA discussion); the relation to ordinal input is mentioned (intensities inferred from ordinal data) but not defined.

C4.2.quote: Assuming voters exhibit dichotomous preferences, AV possesses a variety of desirable properties
C4.2.note: Term used when citing prior work; the two classes are not explained. The paper's own AV analysis uses cut-off levels on rankings instead.

C5.1.quote: brings not forth a polarizing candidate as the electoral winner.
C5.1.note: Results evaluate rules by property PPC (non-election of polarizing candidates) and Condorcet consistency, not by welfare, efficiency, satisfaction, representation, proportionality or distortion.

VOT.quote_behav: we assume that all voters participate in all rounds and vote
VOT.note: Voters submit their preference rankings sincerely; Sec. 2 also says 'we neglect strategic considerations of voters'. Info NA as behav = NONSTRAT (the paper says voters are perfectly informed about candidates' policy choice, Sec. 2, p. 2).

CAN.note: Candidates serve only as alternatives in the formal model; their incentives to polarize are discussed outside the model.

DES.note: Rule comparison is not modelled as a designer's choice or objective.

C7.1.note: Only voters are present by the C6 definition.

C8.1.note: NA: no type is STRAT or MIXED.

C9.1.note: Claims about incentives created by real electoral rules and which rules are suitable or acceptable.

C9.2.quote: voters’ top (best) preference is always identical with their votes
C9.2.note: Sincere voting (inputs = preferences) is stated. Claims about candidates' incentives to polarize and their benefit from polarizing need an assumption that candidates choose positions strategically and that polarizing shifts the profile in their favour; candidates are not modelled as acting agents and this is not stated.

C10.1.loc: Sec. 1 Introduction; Sec. 2 The model; Sec. 4.3; Sec. 4.4; Sec. 5 Conclusion
C10.1.note: The paper assumes sincere voting rather than declaring a purely procedural reading.

C2.4.reason: The identity of votes and preferences is stated in words and supported by a citation of convention (both coders code C3.3 = CONV), so IDJ fits better than DIST (no separate objects in the model) or IDS (a reason is given).

C4.1.reason: The paper refers to voters' preference intensities, which triggers C4.1, and only mentions without defining that they are inferred from ordinal rankings.
